title: Hypothesis testing as a two-error procedure
dek: A test is a rule that, for each data set, says reject H₀ or not. Size is the Type I probability of that rule. Power is one minus Type II at a specified alternative. A p-value is not the procedure; it is a tail the procedure can use.
story: A hypothesis test starts with two scientific stories written as sets of parameters: H₀ (the restriction you might reject) and H₁ (the alternative you take seriously). A test is a measurable partition of the sample space into a rejection region R and its complement. You do not “accept H₀” in the Neyman–Pearson grammar; you fail to reject it. That wording is pedantic on purpose: absence of evidence is not a proof of the restriction.

Size (Type I error rate) is P(reject H₀ | H₀ true), usually capped at α = 0.05 by convention, not by nature. Power is P(reject H₀ | a named point in H₁). You cannot quote power without an alternative, an n, and a test. Type I and Type II already have a glossary plate; this plate is the procedure those errors belong to.

A p-value is P(discrepancy as large or larger | H₀). Comparing it to α is one way to build R. It is not P(H₀ | data), not an effect size, and not a posterior odds. The p-versus-posterior plate exists because this swap is the most expensive sentence in applied work.
deepTitle: How to write one without theatre
deep: Simple versus simple: Neyman–Pearson lemma says a likelihood-ratio rejection region is most powerful at a given size (own glossary plate). Composite H₀ (θ in a set) needs a maximised null, which is why LRTs, Wald, and score exist.

Pre-specify the discrepancy. Two-sided versus one-sided, LRT versus Wald, permutation versus parametric — each is a different test. Optional stopping without a plan changes the null sampling law of the p-value.
Equivalence and non-inferiority reverse which error is which: you reject a difference larger than a margin. “p > 0.05 therefore equivalent” is not that test.
Multiple testing: each extra test is another chance at Type I. FWER and FDR (own plates) change the error-rate contract. They do not change the definition of a single test.
In TB genomics, H₀ is often “this mutation is not associated with MIC after lineage.” Write the likelihood and the restriction. A starred SNP without a named H₀ is a ranking, not a test.

formulas.label: Size of a test
formulas.note: A property of the rule R, not of one observed y.

formulas.label: Power at a point
formulas.expression: 1 − β(θ₁) = P(Y ∈ R | θ = θ₁ ∈ H₁)
formulas.note: Needs a named alternative. “The study was powered” without θ₁ is a slogan.

visual.caption: From a named H₀ and a discrepancy to a reject / do-not-reject rule. α is a long-run property of that rule under H₀. A p-value is a tail computed on the way; it is not P(H₀ | y).

example.title: A proportion test is a rule, not a vibe
example.setup: H₀: π = 0.05 FQ-R among RR-TB. n = 40, x = 0. Someone says “zero events, so H₀ is true.” Another says “p is small because 0 is far from 0.05.”

steps.title: Write the test
steps.body: X ~ Binomial(40, π) under the iid claim. A one-sided test of H₀: π = 0.05 versus π < 0.05 can use the lower tail P(X ≤ 0 | π = 0.05) = (0.95)⁴⁰ ≈ 0.13. That p-value does not reject at α = 0.05.

steps.title: What “zero events” did not do
steps.body: Failing to reject is compatible with π = 0.05 and with π = 0.01. A confidence interval or a posterior is the object that reports remaining π values. The test only said the lower tail was not rare enough under this H₀.

steps.title: Power needs an alternative
steps.body: Power at π = 0.01 with this n and this tail is modest. If the scientific job was to rule out 5%, you needed a larger n or a different design — that is the power plate, not a smaller α.

example.takeaway: A test is a reject/not rule with a size. Zero events are data, not an automatic proof of H₀.

check.prompt: Failing to reject H₀ at level α means:
choices: The data were not rare enough, under this test, to reject the restriction at the chosen size
check.answer: The data were not rare enough, under this test, to reject the restriction at the chosen size
check.why: Neyman–Pearson grammar does not “accept” H₀. Equivalence needs a different hypothesis.

whyWrong.H₀ has been proven true: Absence of evidence is not proof of the restriction.
whyWrong.P(H₀ | data) > 1 − α: That would be a posterior, which this procedure does not compute.

check.prompt: A test rejects when p ≤ 0.05 and, under a simple H₀, p is Uniform(0,1). The Type I error rate is:
check.why: P(p ≤ 0.05 | H₀) = 0.05 if p is Uniform(0,1) under H₀. That is the size of the rule.

whyWrong.0: A level-α test is allowed to reject true H₀ with probability α.
whyWrong.0.95: That would be 1 − α, a confidence-level number, not this test’s size.

check.prompt: On the testing flow, the p-value node sits before reject/do-not-reject because:
check.figureHint: Tail node feeds both the comparison and Reject.
choices: The p-value is already P(H₀ | y)
The tail is an input you may compare to α to define the rejection region; the decision is the rule, not the tail itself
You must reject whenever a p-value exists
α is computed from the alternative only
check.answer: The tail is an input you may compare to α to define the rejection region; the decision is the rule, not the tail itself
check.why: A p-value can be reported without α. A test is the comparison (or an equivalent critical-value rule).

whyWrong.The p-value is already P(H₀ | y): That is the swap the posterior plate exists to stop.
whyWrong.You must reject whenever a p-value exist: You can report p without a binary decision.
whyWrong.α is computed from the alternative only: α is a null property of the rule.
